text: Over the centuries, these communities moved east into the great plain of the Ganga.
They cleared forests, farmed rice, learned iron, and built kingdoms.
By about 600 BCE, North India had 16 big states.
Society was hardening too into ranked groups of priests, warriors, traders, and workers.
Over many centuries, that system, Varna, would set into the rigid rules of caste.
And then, around two and a half thousand years ago, a king in the foothills of today's Nepal
had a son.
A seer warned him, this boy will become either a great king or a great holy man.
The king wanted a king, so he gave his son Siddhartha a perfect palace.
No sickness, no old age, no death, nothing sad ever.
It worked for twenty-nine years.
Then Siddhartha slipped out, and in one afternoon he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body,
and a calm wandering monk. Soon after he left the palace, his wife and his baby son, to
find out why people suffer. Years later, under a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, he sat down and refused
to get up until he understood. When he rose, he was the Buddha, the awakened one. His answer
There was a middle way, not luxury, not starvation, a calm, kind, disciplined life.
That's the story Buddhists have told for more than two thousand years.
And here's the strange part.
Around the same time, another prince, Mahavira, walked away from his throne too and taught
non-violence to every living thing.
Jainism grew from his teaching.
Two princes, zero palaces, very confused royal parents. Remember our question about robbers?
Here's the one treasure nobody could steal. Ideas. Buddhism would travel from this land
to China, Japan, and all of Southeast Asia, further than any army. But armies were coming
the other way. Far to the west, a young king from Macedonia had just conquered the mightiest
